A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MMAD task, MMA-52 dataset and DSTA method. Their readable text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. V2 ends after references; v3 additionally contains Appendices A–D, assessed against the supplied earlier PDF.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original MMA-52 detection results, comparisons with baselines, adapter and fusion-weight ablations, error analyses and qualitative predictions.

after.justification: V3 retains the original benchmark experiments and additionally reports adapter-placement results, sensitivity analyses and prediction examples in its appendices.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Equations (1)–(3) retain the same adapter framework, spatial and temporal pathways, and learnable fusion weights. Appendix B details the temporal convolution block without establishing a change to the existing method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate micro-action detection on MMA-52, with 6,528 videos, 19,782 instances, 203 subjects and the same action-level and body-level categories. The appendix analyses use this retained coverage; no additional dataset or distinct task scenario is evaluated.

E2.justification: Table 3 retains the same ten baseline methods and backbone assignments, including MS-TCT, PointTAD, TemporalMaxer, Re2TAL and AdaTAD. Table 4 also retains the same full fine-tuning, standard-adapter and TIA comparisons.

E3.justification: V3 introduces controlled adapter placements in VideoMAE-S layers 1–4, 5–8, 9–12 or all layers, plus bucketed normalized-mAP sensitivity evaluation at tIoU=0.5. Existing splits, resolutions, backbone configurations and main evaluation thresholds remain unchanged. The action-to-body label mapping is newly disclosed, rather than an established protocol revision.

E4.justification: V2's fusion-weight ablation in Table 5 is removed, including tests without beta, gamma or both. V3's Appendix C instead adds an adapter-position ablation and normalized-mAP sensitivity analyses for coverage, duration and instance count; Appendix D adds three prediction case studies. This substantially revises the supporting analyses, while retaining the main false-positive and false-negative diagnostics.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. Figure 4 retains the same duration mean-and-standard-deviation reporting. Figure 10's new sensitivity ranges describe differences across data buckets, not statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 3–4 retain their scores, including DSTA's combined AVG values of 23.43 and 25.34. Fusion-weight results are omitted, while new placement results include action-level averages of 10.38, 13.83 and 13.52; Figures 10–11 add diagnostic and qualitative results. Section 5.2 changes AdaTAD's stated best average from 21.08 to 21.80, although its retained VideoMAE-B table entry is 23.08.

T1.justification: The set-prediction formulation and adapter equations are unchanged. The appendices add implementation and empirical-analysis descriptions, without new theorems, assumptions, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: introducing MMAD and MMA-52, proposing DSTA and benchmarking conventional action detectors. Their scientific scope and headline effectiveness claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V3 removes the fusion-weight ablation's interpretation emphasizing spatial information. Appendix C adds interpretations about adapter placement, relative sensitivity to action characteristics and using body-level information to assist action-level detection. It also introduces an inconsistent statement that action-level detection is easier despite reporting higher body-level scores.

D1.justification: Appendices A–B document label IDs matching MA-52, the temporal convolution stack with kernel sizes {1,3,1}, and the use of AdaTAD's loss. Section 5.1 and Appendix B.1 clarify that body-level scores come from mapping action-level predictions. These are additional disclosures; the dataset link and existing training details remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V3 adds supporting citations on micro-gesture learning, motion modeling and bottleneck design, and removes two speech-emotion references. Section 3.3 locally shifts emphasis from prior datasets' privacy restrictions to category limitations. The overall novelty positioning remains stable; the publication update for the prototypical-calibration paper represents the same cited work.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose remain intact. V3 makes limited grammar, terminology and affiliation corrections, adds acknowledgments, and organizes supplementary material into Appendices A–D. It does not extensively rewrite the main narrative.

P2.justification: V3 retains the existing main figures, relocates Table 1 and Figure 5, and adjusts spacing and captions. It removes the original Table 5 and adds a different appendix Table 5 plus Figures 9–11 for architecture details, sensitivity and predictions. These are localized display additions and layout changes.

improvement.justification: V3 modestly improves reproducibility by documenting the temporal block, loss reference and action-to-body scoring procedure, and adds useful placement and sensitivity evidence. These gains are limited by removing the fusion-weight ablation and introducing an inconsistent interpretation of hierarchy-level performance in Appendix C.2. The main benchmark results and central conclusions remain unchanged.
